neolithic-revolution.name: Neolithic Revolution
neolithic-revolution.summary: The wide-scale shift from hunting and gathering to farming and settlement across Afro-Eurasia starting around 11,700 years ago, enabling larger populations despite reducing dietary diversity.

neolithic-greece.name: Neolithic Greece
neolithic-greece.summary: The Neolithic phase of Greek history from about 7000 to 3200 BC, marked by farming, stock-rearing, distinctive house styles, and elaborate art and tool making.

thessaly.name: Thessaly
thessaly.summary: A geographic and administrative region of northern central Greece, formerly known as Aeolia, which became part of the modern Greek state in 1881.

vicia-ervilia.name: Bitter vetch
vicia-ervilia.summary: An ancient Mediterranean legume crop, traditionally grown mainly for animal feed.

hesiod.name: Hesiod
hesiod.summary: Ancient Greek poet active around 750–650 BC, a near-contemporary of Homer, whose surviving works Theogony and Works and Days are major sources on Greek mythology, farming and early cosmology.

tell-archaeology.name: Tell
tell-archaeology.summary: A mound built up from the accumulated debris of successive settlements, most commonly found across the ancient Near East and parts of Europe.

varna-necropolis.name: Varna Necropolis
varna-necropolis.summary: A prehistoric burial site near Varna, Bulgaria, where the oldest known gold treasure and jewelry (4600-4200 BCE) were discovered, including elite graves holding scepters.

megaron.name: Megaron
megaron.summary: The great hall of early Mycenaean and Greek palaces: a rectangular room with a central hearth and columned portico, used for royal functions and court meetings.

chalcolithic.name: Chalcolithic (Copper Age)
chalcolithic.summary: An archaeological period between the Neolithic and Bronze Age marked by growing use of smelted copper, with evidence of copper smelting from as early as about 5000 BCE in parts of Europe.

milos.name: Milos
milos.summary: A volcanic Greek island in the Cyclades, source of famous sculptures including the Venus de Milo, with a population of about 5,193 as of 2021.

franchthi-cave.name: Franchthi Cave
franchthi-cave.summary: Archaeological site on Kiladha Bay in southeastern Greece, occupied as a shelter for about 35,000 years from the Upper Paleolithic through the Neolithic; one of the most studied Stone Age sites in Southeast Europe.

sesklo.name: Sesklo
sesklo.summary: A village near Volos, Greece, and the site of a major Neolithic settlement that flourished before the Bronze Age and the Mycenaean period.

dimini.name: Dimini
dimini.summary: Village near Volos in Thessaly, Greece, site of both a Neolithic settlement and a Mycenaean palace believed to be ancient Iolcos, excavated from the late 19th century onward.

christos-tsountas.name: Christos Tsountas
christos-tsountas.summary: Greek classical archaeologist (1857–1934), a pioneer of Greek prehistory who excavated the citadel of Mycenae and first identified Cycladic culture.

varna-bulgaria.name: Varna
varna-bulgaria.summary: The third-largest city in Bulgaria and a major Black Sea port, historically known as Odessos, near which the ancient Varna gold treasure was discovered.

vin-a-culture.name: Vinča culture
vin-a-culture.summary: Neolithic archaeological culture of Southeast Europe dated to about 5400–4500 BC, known for distinctive pottery, figurines, and the earliest known copper smelting.

divostin.name: Divostin
divostin.summary: Village in Serbia that is the site of a major Neolithic and Bronze Age settlement, yielding over 100,000 objects from the Starčevo and Vinča cultures.

thermoluminescence-dating.name: Thermoluminescence Dating
thermoluminescence-dating.summary: A dating method measuring accumulated radiation to determine when crystalline material was last heated or exposed to sunlight, used on ceramics, lava, and sediments.

pieria-regional-unit.name: Pieria
pieria-regional-unit.summary: A regional unit in Greece's Central Macedonia, home to Mount Olympus and ancient sites like Dion and Pydna, named after the ancient Pieres tribe.

provadia.name: Provadia
provadia.summary: A town in northeastern Bulgaria near the Black Sea coast, historically a customs point known for its salty mineral waters.

demic-diffusion.name: Demic diffusion
demic-diffusion.summary: A model of human migration, developed by Luigi Luca Cavalli-Sforza, describing population growth followed by dispersal and mixing with existing peoples, used to explain the spread of farming.

vin-a-belo-brdo.name: Vinča-Belo Brdo
vin-a-belo-brdo.summary: Archaeological tell site near Belgrade, Serbia, occupied from around 5700 BCE through the Middle Ages; it is the type site that gave the Vinča culture its name.

miloje-vasi.name: Miloje Vasić
miloje-vasi.summary: Serbian archaeologist (1869–1956), regarded as the founder of modern Serbian archaeology, who discovered the Neolithic Vinča culture site in 1905 and began excavating it in 1908.

lepenski-vir.name: Lepenski Vir
lepenski-vir.summary: A Mesolithic-to-Neolithic archaeological site on the Danube in Serbia, spanning roughly 9500 to 5500 BC, known for unique trapezoidal buildings and fish-faced sculptures across one large settlement and ten satellite villages.

varna-culture.name: Varna culture
varna-culture.summary: A Chalcolithic culture of northeastern Bulgaria, dated to about 4500 BCE, known for the world's oldest gold artifacts and rich cemeteries including the Varna Necropolis.

dragoslav-srejovi.name: Dragoslav Srejović
dragoslav-srejovi.summary: Serbian archaeologist, cultural anthropologist and historian (1931–1996), the main excavator of the Lepenski Vir site.

varna-archaeological-museum.name: Varna Archaeological Museum
varna-archaeological-museum.summary: A museum in Varna, Bulgaria, founded in 1888, that displays the Gold of Varna, the oldest known gold treasure in the world, dated 4600-4200 BCE.

vin-a-symbols.name: Vinča symbols
vin-a-symbols.summary: A set of undeciphered symbols found on artifacts of the Neolithic Vinča culture, sometimes described as an early form of proto-writing, used until around 3500 BC.

star-evo-culture.name: Starčevo culture
star-evo-culture.summary: An archaeological culture of Neolithic Southeastern Europe, about 6200 to 4500 BCE, that spread farming and ceramics from Asia Minor into the inland Balkans.

marija-gimbutas.name: Marija Gimbutas
marija-gimbutas.summary: Lithuanian archaeologist and anthropologist known for her research into Neolithic and Bronze Age 'Old Europe' and for the Kurgan hypothesis placing the Proto-Indo-European homeland in the Pontic Steppe.

mavropigi.name: Mavropigi
mavropigi.summary: A village in Greece's Kozani region, near where archaeologists uncovered an intact first-century BC tomb with a unique bronze funeral bier.
